questions.stem: An application running on an Amazon EC2 instance must read objects from a private Amazon S3 bucket. Company policy forbids storing long-lived credentials anywhere on the instance, and the credentials the application uses must be rotated automatically by AWS. What should the solutions architect do?
questions.hint: Think about which mechanism hands short-lived credentials to compute without anyone copying a secret onto the host.

options.text: Attach an IAM role to the instance profile granting read access to that bucket.
options.why: Correct — an instance profile delivers temporary credentials through the instance metadata service, and the SDK refreshes them automatically, so nothing long-lived is stored on disk.

options.text: Turn off Block Public Access so the instance can read the objects freely.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: removing the credential problem by making data public exposes the bucket to the entire internet; Block Public Access is a guardrail, not an access-granting mechanism.

options.text: Create an IAM user and place its access keys in a file on the instance.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: this does work technically, but the access keys are long-lived credentials stored on the host, which is exactly what the policy forbids.

options.text: Create an IAM group with S3 read permissions and add the EC2 instance to that group.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: IAM groups only contain IAM users. An EC2 instance cannot be a member of a group; it receives permissions through a role.

questions.stem: A company runs a MySQL database on a single Amazon RDS instance in one Availability Zone. Management now requires that the loss of the database instance or of its entire Availability Zone be recovered automatically within a few minutes with no committed data lost. The application connects through the RDS endpoint and the team does not want to change application code. Which change meets this requirement?
questions.hint: Focus on which RDS option keeps a second copy written synchronously and fails over on its own.

options.text: Enable a Multi-AZ deployment so RDS keeps a synchronous standby in a second Availability Zone.
options.why: Correct — Multi-AZ replicates writes synchronously to a standby in another AZ and RDS fails the endpoint over automatically, giving no committed data loss and recovery in minutes without code changes.

options.text: Create a cross-Region read replica and promote it by hand whenever the primary stops responding.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: read replicas replicate asynchronously and promotion is a manual step, so recovery is not automatic and recent transactions can be lost.

options.text: Schedule automated snapshots hourly and restore a fresh instance from the newest snapshot.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: snapshots protect the data but restoring is a manual, slow operation and up to an hour of writes would be lost, which fails the no-data-loss requirement.

options.text: Turn on RDS Performance Insights so failing instances are detected and replaced for you.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: Performance Insights is a database performance monitoring tool; it visualises load but performs no failover or instance replacement.

questions.topic: EBS volume types and IOPS vs throughput
questions.stem: A transactional application runs on a single EC2 instance and stores its database on a 500 GiB EBS volume. Monitoring shows the workload steadily needs about 12,000 IOPS and 400 MB/s of throughput. The team wants to meet both figures at the lowest cost without changing the volume size. Which volume configuration should the solutions architect choose?
questions.hint: Consider which SSD volume type lets you set IOPS and throughput as separate dials rather than deriving them from capacity.

options.text: Use a gp3 volume and provision 12,000 IOPS and 400 MB/s separately from the 500 GiB size
options.why: Correct — gp3 decouples performance from capacity: it includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s at any size and can be provisioned up to 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MB/s, so both targets are met on a 500 GiB volume.

options.text: Use an io2 volume provisioned at 12,000 IOPS, which costs more per IOPS than gp3 does
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: io2 can deliver 12,000 IOPS, but it is priced for sub-millisecond consistency and durability that this workload does not require, so it fails the lowest-cost condition.

options.text: Use a gp2 volume sized at 4,000 GiB so the 3 IOPS per GiB rule reaches 12,000 IOPS
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: gp2 does scale at 3 IOPS per GiB, but reaching 12,000 IOPS means paying for 4,000 GiB of unused capacity and the stem forbids changing the volume size.

options.text: Use an st1 throughput-optimized HDD volume, which is built for large sequential streaming reads
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: st1 is an HDD tuned for sequential throughput such as log processing, and it cannot sustain the random IOPS a transactional database issues.

questions.topic: EC2 purchase options for steady load
questions.stem: A company runs a licensing service on 20 always-on EC2 instances. The load has been flat 24/7 for two years and is forecast to stay flat for at least three more. Finance is willing to commit to a fixed hourly spend for a three-year term, but the engineering team expects to move to a newer instance family during that time. The service cannot tolerate interruption. Which purchase option gives the lowest cost while allowing the family change?
questions.hint: Weigh which commitment model stays discounted after the instance family changes.

options.text: Buy a three-year Compute Savings Plan that commits to a fixed hourly spend.
options.why: Correct — a Compute Savings Plan discounts any instance family, size or Region for the committed hourly spend, so the discount survives a family migration.

options.text: Buy three-year Standard Reserved Instances matching the current instance family.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: Standard RIs discount heavily but cannot be exchanged for a different instance family, so the saving is lost at migration.

options.text: Run the whole fleet on Spot Instances and handle the two-minute interruption notice.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: Spot capacity can be reclaimed with only two minutes' warning, which this uninterruptible service cannot absorb.

options.text: Stay On-Demand and create an AWS Budgets alert on monthly EC2 spend.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: a Budgets alert reports spend but applies no discount to a steady, committable workload.

questions.stem: A developer belongs to an IAM group whose attached policy allows s3:* on all buckets. A second identity-based policy attached directly to that developer contains an explicit Deny for s3:DeleteObject on the company logs bucket. Both policies are in the same AWS account as the bucket. What happens when the developer tries to delete an object in the logs bucket?
questions.hint: Recall the fixed order in which allows and denies are combined when several policies apply to one principal.

options.text: The request succeeds, because group policies are evaluated before user policies.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: IAM has no precedence order between group-attached and user-attached policies. All applicable policies are combined into a single evaluation.

options.text: The request succeeds, because the wildcard allow is more specific than the deny.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: specificity does not decide the outcome in IAM. A wildcard allow never outranks an explicit deny on the same action.

options.text: The request is denied, because an explicit deny always overrides any allow.
options.why: Correct — IAM evaluation is deny-by-default: an explicit Deny in any applicable policy wins over every Allow, no matter where the Allow comes from.

options.text: The request succeeds; only a permissions boundary can enforce a deny.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: a permissions boundary caps the maximum permissions an identity can have, but it is not required for an explicit Deny to take effect.

questions.stem: A reporting team runs long read-only SQL queries that slow down the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance serving a busy web application. The reports may safely use data that is a few seconds out of date, and the company wants to remove the reporting load from the primary instance with the least operational effort. What should a solutions architect recommend?
questions.hint: Decide which RDS copy of the data is actually available for applications to query.

options.text: Enable Multi-AZ so that the standby instance absorbs the reporting query workload.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: the classic Multi-AZ standby accepts no connections at all; it exists only for failover, so it cannot serve reports.

options.text: Create a read replica and send the reporting queries to the replica endpoint.
options.why: Correct — a read replica is asynchronously updated and fully queryable, so seconds-old data is acceptable and the primary is freed from the reporting load with minimal effort.

options.text: Resize the primary instance to the largest class available in its instance family.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: a bigger instance masks the contention for a while at higher cost, but reports still compete with production traffic on one instance.

options.text: Restore the newest automated snapshot into a separate instance every morning for reporting.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: this isolates the load but the data is a day old rather than seconds old and the daily restore is manual work.

questions.stem: A media company runs a nightly video transcoding job on EC2. Profiling shows the job pins all vCPUs at 100 percent for six hours straight while using less than 4 GiB of memory and almost no local disk. The team wants the best sustained compute performance per dollar for this run. Which instance family should they select?
questions.hint: Match the instance family to the resource that is actually saturated, and watch for families whose full performance is only temporary.

options.text: Choose R-family memory optimized instances, which raise RAM per vCPU rather than CPU power
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: R-family instances are correct EC2 sizing practice but optimize memory, and this job uses under 4 GiB, so the extra RAM is paid for and unused.

options.text: Choose C-family compute optimized instances, which offer high sustained CPU per dollar
options.why: Correct — compute optimized C-family instances use high-performance processors and give the highest ratio of CPU to cost, which suits a CPU-bound batch job that runs flat out for hours.

options.text: Choose T-family burstable instances and rely on CPU credits to hold full speed for six hours
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: T-family instances earn credits while idle and spend them while busy, so a six-hour full-load run exhausts the balance and drops to baseline or incurs surplus charges.

options.text: Choose I-family storage optimized instances, which add fast local NVMe rather than CPU
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: I-family instances would run the job, but their premium is local NVMe throughput, and the stem states the job uses almost no local disk.

questions.stem: An insurance firm writes claim PDFs to Amazon S3. Documents are read many times during the first 30 days, occasionally read between day 30 and day 90, and after 90 days are almost never read but must be kept for seven years for audit. When an old document is requested, the auditors accept a wait of several hours. Which lifecycle configuration is cheapest while meeting these access needs?
questions.hint: Match each access pattern to the class whose retrieval behaviour it can tolerate.

options.text: Keep objects in S3 Standard for 90 days, then delete them once auditing ends.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: deleting at 90 days breaks the seven-year audit retention the scenario requires.

options.text: Move to S3 Standard-IA at day 30, then S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval at day 90.
options.why: Correct — Standard-IA suits occasional reads and Glacier Flexible Retrieval is far cheaper for archives whose retrieval may take hours.

options.text: Transition to S3 One Zone-IA at day 30 and keep the objects there for the full seven years.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: One Zone-IA costs more than Glacier for a seven-year archive and stores only one Availability Zone copy.

options.text: Transition every object to S3 Glacier Deep Archive on the day it is uploaded.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: Deep Archive is the cheapest tier but its multi-hour restore blocks the heavy reads of the first 30 days.

questions.stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. Auditors require that nobody in any workload account, including that account's own administrators, can stop or delete the AWS CloudTrail trail. The control must apply to every existing and future account in one organizational unit. What should the architect do?
questions.hint: Consider which control sits above account administrators and limits what any principal in the account can ever be granted.

options.text: Attach an IAM policy denying CloudTrail changes to each administrator in every account.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: an account administrator can detach or edit an IAM policy in their own account, so the control is not tamper-proof and must be repeated for every new user.

options.text: Attach a service control policy to the OU denying CloudTrail stop and delete actions.
options.why: Correct — an SCP applies to every principal in every account under the OU, including the account administrators, and new accounts inherit it automatically.

options.text: Attach a service control policy that grants CloudTrail permissions to the OU accounts.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: SCPs never grant permissions. They only set the maximum permissions available; actual access still comes from IAM policies.

options.text: Enable AWS Config rules in each account to record when CloudTrail is turned off.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: AWS Config would detect and report the change after the fact, but it does not prevent an administrator from stopping the trail.

questions.stem: An application uses an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster with one writer instance and two Aurora Replicas spread across Availability Zones. The company requires that write traffic resume automatically about a minute after the writer instance fails, without anyone editing connection strings or restarting the application. Which endpoint should the application use for its write connections?
questions.hint: Think about which Aurora endpoint AWS itself repoints when a new writer is promoted.

options.text: The reader endpoint, which balances connections across the two Aurora Replicas.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: the reader endpoint exists for scaling read traffic and rejects writes, so it cannot carry the write workload.

options.text: The instance endpoint of today's writer, updated by a script after each failover.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: instance endpoints address one specific instance, so this works only after custom automation runs and adds avoidable failure points.

options.text: The cluster endpoint, which Aurora repoints to the promoted writer automatically.
options.why: Correct — the cluster endpoint always resolves to the current writer, so when Aurora promotes a replica the application reconnects to the new writer with no configuration change.

options.text: A Route 53 CNAME record that a Lambda function rewrites whenever a failover event fires.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: this rebuilds a capability Aurora already provides, and DNS caching plus function latency make recovery slower and harder to operate.

questions.topic: EFS vs EBS vs S3 for shared access
questions.stem: A content management platform runs on 20 EC2 instances spread across three Availability Zones. Every instance must read and write the same set of files through a standard file system path, and edits made by one instance must be visible to the others immediately. Which storage design meets this requirement?
questions.hint: Focus on which storage service natively presents one POSIX file system to many instances in different Availability Zones at once.

options.text: Attach one Multi-Attach io2 EBS volume to all 20 instances across the three zones
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: EBS Multi-Attach is real, but it is limited to instances inside a single Availability Zone and needs a cluster-aware file system to avoid corruption.

options.text: Give each instance a private gp3 volume and copy changed files between them on a schedule
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: scheduled copying leaves each instance with a stale local view between runs and invites write conflicts, so it never delivers immediate shared visibility.

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system and mount it from every instance in all three zones
options.why: Correct — EFS is a managed NFS file system with mount targets in multiple Availability Zones, so thousands of instances can read and write the same POSIX tree concurrently.

options.text: Store the files in an S3 bucket and have every instance download a local copy at boot
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: S3 is durable shared storage, but it is an object API rather than a file system path, and a boot-time copy would not reflect later edits by peers.

questions.topic: VPC gateway endpoint versus NAT gateway
questions.stem: A data pipeline runs on EC2 instances in private subnets and writes roughly 40 TB per month to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region. All of that traffic currently leaves through a NAT gateway, and the NAT data-processing charge now dominates the monthly bill. The instances need no other internet access. Which change removes those charges at the lowest cost?
questions.hint: Consider which connectivity option for in-Region S3 traffic carries no hourly or per-GB fee.

options.text: Move the EC2 instances into public subnets with public IPs to reach S3 directly.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: it does avoid NAT fees but exposes the pipeline hosts to the internet and still uses public-path routing.

options.text: Place a second NAT gateway in each Availability Zone to spread the traffic.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: NAT data-processing is billed per GB regardless of how many gateways exist, so cost rises rather than falls.

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and route the subnets' S3 traffic to it.
options.why: Correct — gateway endpoints for S3 carry no hourly or per-GB charge and keep the traffic off the NAT gateway entirely.

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination bucket for the uploads.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: Transfer Acceleration speeds long-distance uploads for a fee and does nothing about NAT charges.

questions.stem: A startup created its first AWS account and its two founders have been performing all daily administration while signed in as the account root user. A security reviewer flags this as the largest single risk in the account. What should the founders do about the root user going forward?
questions.hint: Focus on what the root user can never be restricted from doing, and how often it should actually be used.

options.text: Delete the root user once an IAM administrator exists, removing the risk entirely.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: the root user is part of the account and cannot be deleted. It can only be secured and then left unused.

options.text: Enable MFA on the root user and use IAM identities for daily administration.
options.why: Correct — MFA protects the one identity that cannot be limited by IAM policies, and moving day-to-day work to IAM identities keeps root credentials out of routine use.

options.text: Rotate the root user password every thirty days and keep using it for daily work.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: rotation is reasonable hygiene, but continuing daily use of an identity with unrestricted power leaves the underlying risk in place.

options.text: Attach an IAM policy to the root user to restrict what it can do.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: identity-based policies cannot be attached to the root user, and IAM policies do not limit root within its own account.

questions.stem: A gaming company stores player profiles in one Amazon DynamoDB table in us-east-1. Players in Europe report high latency on both reads and writes. The company wants players in eu-west-1 to read and write to a local copy of the data, with changes replicated between the two Regions automatically and the workload surviving the loss of either Region. Which approach meets these requirements?
questions.hint: Separate features that cache or index data in one Region from features that place data in another Region.

options.text: Deploy DynamoDB Accelerator in eu-west-1 in front of the existing us-east-1 table.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: DAX is an in-Region read cache; it does not accelerate writes and it cannot place data in a second Region.

options.text: Convert the table into a DynamoDB global table with a replica in eu-west-1.
options.why: Correct — global tables create an active-active multi-Region replica set, so each Region serves local reads and writes and DynamoDB replicates changes between them.

options.text: Turn on point-in-time recovery and restore a copy of the table into eu-west-1.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: point-in-time recovery is a backup mechanism that produces a one-off restored table with no ongoing replication between Regions.

options.text: Add a global secondary index to the table so European queries are served from Europe.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: a global secondary index is global across partitions, not across Regions, and it lives in the same Region as the base table.

questions.stem: A data team uploads 40 GB research archives from an EC2 instance to an S3 bucket in the same Region. Single PUT requests frequently fail after 30 minutes of transfer, forcing the whole file to be re-sent, and each attempt uses only a fraction of the available bandwidth. Which change best improves upload speed and resilience?
questions.hint: Think about whether the object can be split so that parallelism and retries operate on something smaller than the whole file.

options.text: Use multipart upload to send parts in parallel and re-send only the parts that fail
options.why: Correct — multipart upload splits the object into independently uploaded parts, so several parts move at once to use the bandwidth and a failure only costs one part rather than 40 GB.

options.text: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration so the archives travel over the CloudFront edge network
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: Transfer Acceleration helps clients that are far from the bucket, but the instance is already in the same Region and it does nothing about restart cost.

options.text: Turn on S3 Versioning so that each failed upload is retained as an earlier object version
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: versioning keeps history of successfully written objects; a failed upload never becomes a version, so it neither speeds transfers nor avoids re-sending data.

options.text: Write the archives to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class to cut transfer cost
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: storage classes change the cost and retrieval time of stored data, not the mechanics of the upload, and the stem asks about speed and resilience.

questions.stem: A media company renders video frames from a queue on EC2. Each frame takes about four minutes, progress is checkpointed, and any frame lost mid-render is simply put back on the queue and rendered again. The batch only has to finish some time within 24 hours, and the fleet grows and shrinks between 50 and 400 instances depending on queue depth. Which EC2 purchase option gives the lowest cost for this fleet?
questions.hint: Focus on how much interruption the workload can absorb before cost even matters.

options.text: Run the render fleet on On-Demand Instances and stop them once the queue is drained.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: On-Demand avoids any commitment but charges full list price for work that tolerates interruption.

options.text: Buy one-year Standard Reserved Instances sized for the fleet's 400-instance peak.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: reservations only pay off on steady usage, so a fleet that often sits at 50 instances wastes most of the commitment.

options.text: Run the render fleet on Spot Instances and re-queue any frame that is interrupted.
options.why: Correct — Spot offers the deepest EC2 discount and the two-minute interruption notice is harmless for checkpointed frames that can be rendered again.

options.text: Run the render fleet on Dedicated Hosts to get per-socket visibility for the renderers.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: Dedicated Hosts exist for licence and tenancy control and are among the costliest ways to buy EC2 capacity.

questions.stem: A regulated customer storing data in Amazon S3 must be able to prove it controls the encryption key: it needs to edit the key's access policy, revoke all access to the key immediately, and see an audit record of every use of the key. Which key choice satisfies these requirements?
questions.hint: Ask which key type exposes a policy document the customer can write and disable on demand.

options.text: An AWS managed KMS key, since AWS rotates it and logs its usage for you.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: an AWS managed key does log usage, but its key policy cannot be edited and the customer cannot disable it, so key control cannot be proven.

options.text: An AWS owned key used by SSE-S3, which encrypts every object at rest by default.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: SSE-S3 keys are owned and managed entirely by AWS. They are not visible in KMS, have no customer-editable policy, and their use is not logged per request.

options.text: A customer managed KMS key with a key policy the customer owns and edits.
options.why: Correct — a customer managed key exposes an editable key policy, can be disabled to revoke all use immediately, and records every cryptographic operation in CloudTrail.

options.text: An AWS Secrets Manager secret holding the key material used to encrypt objects.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: Secrets Manager stores credentials and strings, it is not a cryptographic key store, and S3 server-side encryption cannot consume a secret as its key.

questions.stem: A web application runs on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Occasionally the web server process crashes while the instance itself keeps running, so the load balancer marks the target unhealthy and stops sending it traffic, yet Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling never replaces the instance. The team wants such instances terminated and replaced automatically. What should they do?
questions.hint: Consider which signal the Auto Scaling group is currently allowed to act on.

options.text: Raise the desired capacity of the group so that healthy instances always outnumber failed ones.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: extra capacity hides the symptom and costs more, while broken instances accumulate in the group and are never replaced.

options.text: Change the group's health check type to ELB so failed target checks force replacement.
options.why: Correct — with the ELB health check type the Auto Scaling group treats a load balancer target failure as an instance failure, terminating and relaunching the instance automatically.

options.text: Attach a target tracking scaling policy based on average CPU utilization to the group.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: target tracking adjusts how many instances run for a load level; it never evaluates whether an existing instance is healthy.

options.text: Shorten the EC2 status check interval so that instance failures are noticed sooner.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: EC2 status checks watch the hypervisor and instance operating system, not the application process, and their interval is not configurable.

questions.stem: A retailer serves product images and CSS files directly from an S3 bucket in eu-west-1. Shoppers in Asia and South America report that pages take several seconds to render, and bucket metrics show the same few thousand objects being fetched over and over from far-away networks. Which change most reduces the latency these shoppers see?
questions.hint: The objects are identical for every viewer, so ask what a caching layer close to the viewer would remove from each request.

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket, which speeds long-distance transfers only
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: Transfer Acceleration routes traffic over the AWS edge network but stores no copy at the edge, so every request still travels back to eu-west-1.

options.text: Replicate the bucket to several Regions and let shoppers choose the nearest bucket by hand
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: cross-Region replication does place data closer, but manual bucket selection pushes routing onto the shopper and leaves no automatic caching or failover.

options.text: Place the bucket behind an Application Load Balancer to spread requests over more targets
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: an ALB distributes load among compute targets and does not front S3 or cache content, so it cannot shorten the network path for distant viewers.

options.text: Create a CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as origin and serve viewers from it
options.why: Correct — CloudFront caches the objects at edge locations near Asia and South America, so repeat requests are answered locally instead of crossing the ocean to eu-west-1 each time.

questions.topic: DynamoDB capacity mode for unpredictable traffic
questions.stem: A startup launches a mobile game backed by an Amazon DynamoDB table. Traffic is unpredictable: some hours see almost no requests, while a single viral post can drive a twentyfold spike within minutes. The team has no usage history on which to base a capacity estimate and does not want to tune scaling settings. Which table capacity choice keeps cost aligned with actual usage?
questions.hint: Consider which capacity mode charges for traffic that happened rather than traffic that was planned.

options.text: Use provisioned capacity sized for the largest spike the team can imagine today.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: provisioning for a peak bills that peak around the clock, including the many hours the table is nearly idle.

options.text: Use on-demand capacity mode so the table bills only for requests actually made.
options.why: Correct — on-demand mode charges per read and write request and absorbs sudden spikes instantly, which suits traffic with no usage history.

options.text: Use provisioned capacity with auto scaling set to a narrow target range.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: auto scaling adjusts over minutes and still needs sensible floor and ceiling values the team cannot yet estimate.

options.text: Use provisioned capacity and raise the write limits manually when a spike is reported.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: a spike is over long before an operator reacts, so the table throttles players while still costing more than it should.

questions.stem: A compliance standard requires that the cryptographic material behind a symmetric encryption key changes once per year. Data already encrypted with older material must continue to decrypt with no re-encryption work and no application change. Which option meets this with the least operational effort?
questions.hint: Consider whether the key identifier the applications reference has to change at all.

options.text: Enable automatic annual rotation on the existing customer managed KMS key.
options.why: Correct — KMS generates new backing key material yearly while keeping the same key ID and ARN, and it retains older material so previously encrypted data still decrypts.

options.text: Schedule deletion of the KMS key yearly so a fresh key is made.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: deleting a KMS key permanently destroys the material, making every object encrypted under it unrecoverable rather than rotating it.

options.text: Create a new KMS key every year and re-encrypt all existing objects with it.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: manual rotation does change the material, but it forces a bulk re-encryption job and application updates, which the requirement rules out.

options.text: Import new key material yearly and re-point each application to the new key.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: imported material is supported, but it puts the generation, storage and yearly import burden on the customer instead of on KMS.

questions.stem: A solutions architect is designing a two-tier web application in a single AWS Region. EC2 web servers sit behind an Application Load Balancer, and the business requires the site to stay reachable if one Availability Zone becomes unavailable. The team wants the simplest design that satisfies this requirement. Which configuration should the architect choose?
questions.hint: Remember what an Application Load Balancer can and cannot span, and which subnets it will actually use.

options.text: Place instances in two Availability Zones and enable both AZ subnets on the load balancer.
options.why: Correct — an ALB is a Regional service that spreads nodes across the subnets you enable, so with targets in two AZs it keeps routing traffic when one AZ fails.

options.text: Place all instances in one Availability Zone and add a second balancer in another zone.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: a second balancer with no targets behind it cannot serve requests, so losing the single AZ still takes the application offline.

options.text: Place instances in two Availability Zones but enable only the primary subnet on the balancer.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: the load balancer only sends traffic to enabled subnets, so the instances in the second AZ sit idle and provide no protection.

options.text: Place instances in two Regions and register them with the same Application Load Balancer.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: an Application Load Balancer is Regional and cannot register targets that live in another Region.

questions.stem: A mobile game needs an in-memory cache that keeps a live leaderboard ordered by player score and answers rank queries in under a millisecond. The cached leaderboard must also survive the loss of a single cache node without being rebuilt from scratch. Which caching option meets these needs?
questions.hint: Compare what data structures each in-memory engine offers and whether it can replicate its data to another node.

options.text: Use ElastiCache for Memcached, whose multithreaded nodes hold simple key and value pairs
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: Memcached is a genuine ElastiCache engine, but it stores only opaque values and offers no replication, so ranked queries and node failure both break it.

options.text: Use ElastiCache for Redis, which provides sorted sets plus replicas for automatic failover
options.why: Correct — Redis sorted sets maintain score ordering natively for fast rank lookups, and a replica in another Availability Zone can be promoted so the cached data survives a node loss.

options.text: Use ElastiCache for Memcached and add many more nodes so a failure loses a smaller share of keys
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: spreading keys over more Memcached nodes shrinks the blast radius but still loses whatever the failed node held, and it adds no ordering capability at all.

options.text: Use DynamoDB Accelerator, an in-memory cache that fronts reads of DynamoDB tables
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: DAX is a fast in-memory cache, but it only caches DynamoDB item and query results and cannot maintain an arbitrary sorted leaderboard structure.

questions.topic: EBS volume type cost versus performance
questions.stem: An application server keeps its database on a 4 TiB Amazon EBS io1 volume with 8,000 provisioned IOPS. A month of CloudWatch metrics shows the volume never exceeds 5,000 IOPS or 200 MiB/s of throughput, and the team confirms the workload does not need consistent sub-millisecond latency. The volume must stay durable and support random reads and writes. Which change lowers the storage bill while still meeting the observed demand?
questions.hint: Compare what each volume type charges for capacity and for performance against the numbers actually measured.

options.text: Lower the io1 volume's provisioned IOPS from 8,000 to the observed 5,000.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: trimming IOPS helps a little, but io1 still bills a premium per GiB and per provisioned IOPS compared with gp3.

options.text: Migrate the volume to sc1 cold HDD storage to get the lowest available price per GiB.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: sc1 is priced for sequential, throughput-heavy access and cannot sustain thousands of random database IOPS.

options.text: Take a daily snapshot of the volume and delete the older snapshots each week.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: snapshot hygiene trims backup spend but leaves the volume's own capacity and IOPS charges untouched.

options.text: Migrate the volume to gp3 and provision the extra IOPS and throughput it needs.
options.why: Correct — gp3 costs less per GiB than io1 and lets IOPS and throughput be raised independently to the measured 5,000 IOPS and 200 MiB/s.

questions.stem: An organization owns hundreds of Amazon S3 buckets and developers create new ones weekly. Security wants one control that stops any current or future bucket in the account from being made publicly readable, regardless of the bucket policies or object ACLs developers write. What should be configured?
questions.hint: Look for the setting that overrides permissive policies rather than competing with them.

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning on all buckets so public objects can be rolled back.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: versioning protects against overwrite and deletion, but it has no effect on who is allowed to read an object.

options.text: Turn on S3 Block Public Access at the account level for all four settings.
options.why: Correct — the account-level setting overrides bucket policies and ACLs that would grant public access, and it automatically covers buckets created later.

options.text: Write a bucket policy on each bucket denying requests from anonymous callers.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: per-bucket policies can work, but they must be written on every new bucket and a developer with bucket permissions can remove them.

options.text: Enable default encryption with SSE-KMS on every bucket in this account.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: default encryption is good practice for data at rest, but it does not control whether an object is publicly readable.

questions.stem: A company stores contract documents in an Amazon S3 bucket. Users sometimes overwrite a document with a bad copy or delete one by accident, and the business requires that any earlier copy of a single object can be restored within minutes without custom scripts. Which action meets this requirement?
questions.hint: Think about what Amazon S3 retains when the same object key is written or deleted twice.

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration so that document uploads finish faster for remote users.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads over long distances; it keeps no earlier copy of an object and cannot undo an overwrite.

options.text: Enable versioning on the bucket so every overwrite or delete preserves the earlier object version.
options.why: Correct — with versioning each PUT stores a new version and a delete adds a delete marker, so an administrator can restore the previous version of any key in seconds.

options.text: Configure Cross-Region Replication to a bucket in a second Region and copy an object back whenever a user reports a mistake.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: replication copies the bad overwrite to the destination as well, so without versioning there is still no good copy left to retrieve.

options.text: Add a lifecycle rule that moves objects to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval class after 30 days.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: lifecycle transitions reduce storage cost for ageing data but they never retain a prior copy of an object that was replaced.

questions.topic: RDS read replicas for read scaling
questions.stem: An online catalogue uses a Multi-AZ Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance. A new reporting dashboard runs heavy read-only queries that drive primary CPU to 90 percent and slow customer checkouts. The reports may show data that is a few seconds old. Which change offloads the reporting traffic?
questions.hint: Ask which RDS feature adds a separately queryable endpoint rather than only protecting against failure.

options.text: Point the dashboard at the Multi-AZ standby instance so reads leave the primary alone
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: the Multi-AZ standby exists for failover only and accepts no client connections, so it cannot serve the dashboard's read queries.

options.text: Put an RDS Proxy in front of the database so dashboard connections are pooled and reused
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: RDS Proxy manages connection pooling and failover speed, but every pooled query still executes on the same primary CPU that is saturated.

options.text: Create a read replica of the instance and send the dashboard queries to its own endpoint
options.why: Correct — a read replica asynchronously copies the primary and serves read-only queries from its own endpoint, so reporting load moves off the primary and slight staleness is acceptable.

options.text: Move the primary to a larger instance class with more vCPUs and memory to absorb the reports
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: scaling up buys headroom, but reporting and checkout traffic keep competing on one instance and the next report growth repeats the problem.

questions.topic: CloudFront to cut origin data transfer
questions.stem: A news site serves images and short video clips straight from an Amazon S3 bucket to readers worldwide. About 90 percent of requests are for the same few hundred popular files, the monthly bill is dominated by data transfer out to the internet, and readers in distant Regions complain of slow loads. Which change reduces the data transfer charges the most?
questions.hint: Consider where repeated requests for the same file could be answered instead of at the origin bucket.

options.text: Move the objects to S3 Standard-IA to cut the per-GB storage price.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: a cheaper storage class leaves egress charges unchanged and adds retrieval fees to these frequently read files.

options.text: Put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket as its origin.
options.why: Correct — the edge cache answers repeat requests without touching S3, and data transfer from S3 to CloudFront is not charged, so origin egress falls sharply.

options.text: Replicate the bucket into three more Regions and route readers to the nearest copy.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: extra Regions shorten the distance but multiply storage and replication cost while every Region still pays internet egress.

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket so repeated objects are stored once.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: versioning retains extra copies of overwritten objects, increasing storage rather than deduplicating or reducing transfer.

questions.stem: A media application must let one signed-in customer download a single private S3 object during the next 15 minutes. The bucket must remain private to everyone else, and no new IAM identity may be created for the customer. Which approach meets the requirement?
questions.hint: Think about how an existing permitted identity can lend its access for a limited window on one object.

options.text: Grant public read on that single object and remove the grant after 15 minutes.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: a public object is readable by anyone who learns the URL during the window, and the removal step is a manual process that can fail.

options.text: Create a temporary IAM user with read access to the object and email its access keys.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: it would grant access, but it creates the IAM identity the requirement forbids and distributes long-lived credentials by email.

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket to shorten the download window.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance transfers over the edge network; it is a performance feature and grants no access.

options.text: Generate a presigned S3 URL with a 15-minute expiry and send it to the customer.
options.why: Correct — a presigned URL carries the signature of an already-permitted identity, is scoped to one object and operation, and stops working when the expiry passes.

questions.stem: A company serves its public website from EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer and keeps a read-only static copy of the site in an Amazon S3 website bucket. If the main site stops answering health checks, visitors must be sent to the static copy automatically within a few minutes. Which Amazon Route 53 configuration meets this requirement?
questions.hint: Consider which routing policy is designed to pair a health-checked primary target with a standby target.

options.text: Create weighted records that send ten percent of all visitor traffic to the static copy at all times.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: weights split traffic by a fixed ratio, so most visitors still reach the broken site when the main endpoint fails.

options.text: Create latency-based records for both endpoints so that each visitor reaches whichever copy answers fastest.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: latency routing optimises response time between Regions and does not express a primary and standby relationship.

options.text: Create a simple record for the load balancer and lower its time to live to sixty seconds.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: a short TTL only speeds up how fast clients notice a record change; nothing changes the record when the site fails.

options.text: Create failover records with a health check on the load balancer as primary and the bucket as secondary.
options.why: Correct — failover routing returns the secondary record as soon as the health check on the primary fails, so visitors reach the static copy without manual action.

questions.stem: A genomics pipeline runs on EC2 and writes about 2 TB of intermediate files during each analysis, then deletes them when the run finishes. The step is bottlenecked on local write speed, and losing the intermediate files simply means rerunning the job. Which storage choice gives the fastest writes at the lowest cost?
questions.hint: Weigh how much the workload actually needs durability against which storage sits physically closest to the instance.

options.text: Write the intermediate files to the NVMe instance store volumes on the EC2 host itself
options.why: Correct — instance store volumes are physically attached to the host, so they deliver very high write speed at no extra charge, and their loss on stop or failure is acceptable here.

options.text: Write the intermediate files to a 2 TB io2 volume provisioned at its maximum IOPS rating
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: io2 delivers strong consistent IOPS over the network, but paying for its durability and provisioned IOPS is wasted on files that are deleted every run.

options.text: Write the intermediate files to an EFS file system mounted from the analysis instance
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: EFS shines when many instances share one file tree, and its NFS network path adds latency that a single-writer scratch workload does not need.

options.text: Write the intermediate files to an S3 bucket and read them back through the S3 API as needed
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: S3 is durable and cheap to store in, but it is an object store reached over HTTP rather than a local disk, so per-file write latency rises sharply.

questions.topic: Aurora Serverless for intermittent database load
questions.stem: A software company runs an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster behind an internal reporting tool. The tool is busy for roughly two hours each weekday morning and sits essentially idle for the rest of the day and all weekend. The cluster is provisioned for the morning burst, so most of the capacity is paid for but unused, and the team does not want to change the application code. Which option lowers the database cost?
questions.hint: Ask whether the database capacity can shrink on its own during the many idle hours.

options.text: Convert the cluster to Aurora Serverless v2 so database capacity follows demand.
options.why: Correct — Serverless v2 scales capacity units up for the morning burst and down while idle, so the company pays close to what it actually uses.

options.text: Add two Aurora read replicas so the morning burst is spread across them.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: replicas add read capacity and two more billed instances, which raises the cost of the idle hours instead of lowering it.

options.text: Stop the cluster every evening and start it again before the morning burst.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: it does trim idle hours but needs scheduling, and a stopped Aurora cluster restarts by itself after seven days.

options.text: Buy a three-year Reserved Instance covering the current provisioned instance size.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: a reservation discounts an oversized instance and locks in three years of capacity that is idle most of the week.

questions.stem: Objects in an Amazon S3 bucket must be encrypted at rest, and the security team must be able to see a CloudTrail record of every decryption of those objects, showing which principal requested it. Which server-side encryption option should be chosen?
questions.hint: Ask which encryption option involves a separately auditable key service on each request.

options.text: SSE-S3, because the keys it uses are also written into CloudTrail events.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: SSE-S3 keys are handled entirely inside S3 and are never exposed or logged as individual key-usage events.

options.text: SSE-S3 combined with S3 server access logging on the target bucket.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: server access logging records object requests, but it reports no key operations, so decryption by key cannot be audited.

options.text: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key, which records each key use in CloudTrail.
options.why: Correct — every Decrypt call to KMS is logged in CloudTrail with the calling principal, the key ID and the encryption context, giving per-request auditability.

options.text: Client-side encryption using a key stored in the application configuration file.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: client-side encryption does protect the data, but a key held in a config file produces no AWS-side audit trail and adds key handling risk.

questions.stem: An application's web tier sends image-processing jobs straight to a fleet of EC2 worker instances over HTTP. When a worker crashes or is restarted during a deployment, the jobs it was holding are lost and customers must resubmit them. The company wants pending jobs to survive worker failures and be processed once a worker returns. What should a solutions architect recommend?
questions.hint: Think about where a request needs to live while no worker is available to accept it.

options.text: Place an Amazon SQS queue between the tiers so workers poll jobs and delete them after processing.
options.why: Correct — a queue stores each message durably until a worker deletes it, so a job whose worker dies becomes visible again and is picked up by another worker later.

options.text: Put the workers in an Auto Scaling group so that a failed instance is replaced automatically.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: replacement restores capacity but the jobs that the failed instance was holding in memory are already gone.

options.text: Publish each job to an Amazon SNS topic that immediately pushes every message to the worker instances over HTTP endpoints.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: SNS pushes to subscribers rather than holding work for absent consumers, so a job aimed at a stopped worker is still not processed.

options.text: Enable termination protection on the worker instances so that deployments cannot stop them.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: termination protection only blocks the terminate API call; it does not stop crashes, reboots, or in-flight work being lost.

questions.stem: A web tier of fixed-size EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer runs at 20 percent CPU overnight and times out during a two-hour lunchtime peak that varies day to day. The team wants capacity to follow demand automatically without anyone predicting the peak. What should they implement?
questions.hint: Distinguish policies that react to a live metric from those that need someone to know the timing in advance.

options.text: Configure an Auto Scaling group with a target tracking policy on average CPU utilization
options.why: Correct — target tracking adds and removes instances to hold average CPU at the chosen target, so the group grows through an unpredictable lunchtime peak and shrinks again overnight.

options.text: Configure an Auto Scaling group with a scheduled action adding instances at lunchtime
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: scheduled scaling works when the timing is known, but the stem says the peak varies daily, so a fixed schedule over-provisions or falls short.

options.text: Replace the instances with one much larger instance type sized for the busiest recorded day
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: a bigger instance covers the peak but keeps paying for that size all night and reintroduces a single point of failure behind the load balancer.

options.text: Enable cross-zone load balancing on the Application Load Balancer to even out request spread
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: even request distribution is useful, but spreading the same overload across the same fixed fleet adds no capacity during the peak.

questions.stem: A finance team reviews a bill showing 60 m5.4xlarge EC2 instances running a line-of-business application. CloudWatch reports average CPU utilisation of 6 percent and a peak of 14 percent, with memory use well under half of what is allocated. The workload is steady, cannot tolerate interruption, and will keep running for years. What should the team do first to cut cost with the least risk?
questions.hint: Decide whether to change what is being paid for or how much capacity is being run in the first place.

options.text: Buy three-year Reserved Instances for the 60 m5.4xlarge instances now.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: committing for three years to oversized instances locks in the waste, since the discount applies to capacity nobody uses.

options.text: Move the 60 instances onto Spot capacity to take the deepest discount.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: Spot is cheapest but reclaims capacity on two minutes' notice, which this uninterruptible application cannot accept.

options.text: Right-size the instances to a smaller type before committing to any discount.
options.why: Correct — utilisation data already shows the instances are far too large, and shrinking them cuts the bill immediately and makes any later commitment smaller.

options.text: Enable detailed CloudWatch monitoring on every instance to keep watching utilisation.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: it adds a per-instance charge for finer metrics when the existing data is already conclusive about oversizing.

questions.stem: A single malicious IP address is repeatedly probing web servers spread across a public subnet. The team wants to block traffic from that one address for the entire subnet, before it can reach any instance in it. Which control should be used?
questions.hint: One of the two VPC firewalls supports deny rules and applies at the subnet edge.

options.text: A network ACL rule on the subnet that denies traffic from that IP address.
options.why: Correct — network ACLs are stateless subnet-level firewalls that support explicit deny rules, so the traffic is dropped before reaching any instance in the subnet.

options.text: A security group inbound rule that denies traffic from that IP address.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: security group rules are allow-only. There is no deny rule, so a specific address cannot be blocked this way.

options.text: A security group referencing the address, applied to each instance separately.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: even if allow rules were narrowed, the change would have to be applied per instance rather than once at the subnet boundary.

options.text: A route table entry sending that source address to a blackhole destination.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: route tables match on destination, not source, so they cannot be used to filter traffic arriving from a particular client.

questions.stem: A company runs EC2 instances with Amazon EBS volumes, an Amazon RDS database, and an Amazon EFS file system. Auditors now require a daily backup of all three resource types with 35-day retention, scheduled and reported from a single place. The operations team currently maintains its own snapshot scripts and wants to stop doing so. Which approach meets the requirement with the least ongoing effort?
questions.hint: Look for the managed service whose purpose is scheduling and retaining backups across several AWS services.

options.text: Enable versioning on an Amazon S3 bucket and have each server copy its data there nightly.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: bucket versioning protects objects already in S3 and provides no scheduling, retention, or restore path for EBS, RDS, or EFS resources.

options.text: Write an EventBridge rule that triggers a Lambda function to snapshot each resource and delete the expired ones.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: this can work but it recreates a managed capability in custom code that the team must patch, monitor, and audit itself.

options.text: Create an AWS Backup plan with a daily schedule and a 35-day retention rule for the resources.
options.why: Correct — AWS Backup applies one policy with its own schedule and retention to EBS, RDS, and EFS together and reports on every job from a central console.

options.text: Turn on Multi-AZ for the database and mount the file system from two Availability Zones.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: spreading live copies across zones protects against hardware failure but keeps no point-in-time history, so a bad change is copied everywhere.

questions.stem: A product catalogue stores items in a DynamoDB table. The same few thousand popular items are read tens of thousands of times per second, and the team wants those repeat reads answered in microseconds rather than single-digit milliseconds while keeping application changes small. What should they add?
questions.hint: Look for the caching layer that speaks the same API as the database it sits in front of.

options.text: Add a global secondary index on the item identifier so lookups scan fewer table records
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: a GSI supports queries on non-key attributes, and lookups by primary key already hit one item, so it adds no speed for these reads.

options.text: Switch the catalogue read calls to eventually consistent reads on the DynamoDB table
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: eventually consistent reads cost half as much and are slightly faster, yet they still return in milliseconds, not the microseconds required.

options.text: Put an ElastiCache for Redis cluster in front and add cache handling code to the application
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: Redis can cache the items, but the team must write lookup, population and invalidation logic, which conflicts with keeping code changes small.

options.text: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator cluster and point the existing DynamoDB client at its endpoint
options.why: Correct — DAX is an in-memory cache that speaks the DynamoDB API, so cached item reads return in microseconds after only an endpoint change in the client.

questions.topic: S3 Intelligent-Tiering for unknown access patterns
questions.stem: A research group uploads several million data files to Amazon S3 every month, and every file is larger than 1 MB. Some files are read almost daily for years while others are never opened again, and nobody can predict in advance which will be which. All files must stay immediately available, the bill should drop automatically as files go cold, and the group refuses to pay a retrieval fee when a cold file is suddenly needed. Which storage class fits?
questions.hint: Look for the class that reacts to observed access on its own rather than to a schedule you must define.

options.text: Use S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for every file the group uploads.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: it is cheap for rarely read data but charges a per-GB retrieval fee that the frequently read files would incur constantly.

options.text: Use S3 Standard and add a lifecycle rule that expires objects after 30 days.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: expiration deletes objects outright, destroying files the group still reads years after upload.

options.text: Use S3 One Zone-IA and accept the loss of files if an Availability Zone fails.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: One Zone-IA saves money by dropping redundancy, yet still charges retrieval fees and assumes a known access pattern.

options.text: Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering and let it move objects between access tiers.
options.why: Correct — it shifts each object between tiers based on observed access for a small monitoring fee, and charges no retrieval fee when a cold object is read.

questions.stem: Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet must call Amazon S3 in the same Region. The company forbids any route to the internet from that subnet, including through a NAT gateway. Which change lets the instances reach S3 while keeping the traffic on the AWS network?
questions.hint: Consider which connectivity option adds a prefix-list route instead of an internet path.

options.text: Add a NAT gateway in a public subnet and route all S3 traffic through it instead.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: a NAT gateway is the usual way to reach S3 from a private subnet, but it sends traffic out to the internet, which the requirement forbids.

options.text: Attach an internet gateway to the VPC and give the instances public IPs.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: this makes the subnet public and exposes the instances, the opposite of the stated constraint.

options.text: Set up a VPN connection from the VPC to the S3 regional public endpoint.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: Site-to-Site VPN connects a VPC to on-premises networks; it cannot terminate on an AWS service endpoint.

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and add it to the subnet's route table.
options.why: Correct — a gateway endpoint adds a route to the S3 prefix list, so requests stay on the AWS network with no internet gateway or NAT gateway involved.

questions.stem: A company must be able to bring its application back up in a second AWS Region after a Regional outage. The business accepts a recovery time of up to eight hours and the loss of up to 24 hours of data. Cost must be kept as low as possible, and no application servers may run in the second Region during normal operation. Which disaster recovery strategy should a solutions architect choose?
questions.hint: Match the tolerated downtime and data loss to the cheapest strategy that still satisfies both numbers.

options.text: Pilot light: keep a replicated database and core servers idle in the second Region.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: pilot light recovers far faster than needed while paying for replication and idle resources the stated eight-hour target does not require.

options.text: Backup and restore: copy daily backups to the second Region and deploy the stack after a disaster.
options.why: Correct — restoring from a daily backup fits an eight-hour recovery time and a 24-hour data loss allowance while costing only backup storage between disasters.

options.text: Warm standby: run a scaled-down but always-on copy of the environment in the second Region and scale it up on failover.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: an always-on second environment far exceeds the recovery targets and carries continuous compute cost the company wants to avoid.

options.text: Multi-AZ: deploy every tier across Availability Zones so the application survives the outage.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: Availability Zones are all inside one Region, so a Multi-AZ design does not protect the workload from a Regional outage at all.

questions.stem: A research team runs a tightly coupled simulation on 12 EC2 instances that exchange messages continuously. The job finishes far slower than expected, and profiling blames node-to-node network latency. The team accepts that all 12 instances will sit in one Availability Zone. What should they configure?
questions.hint: Placement groups differ in whether they pull instances together or push them apart on the underlying hardware.

options.text: Launch the 12 instances into a spread placement group across distinct underlying hardware
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: a spread placement group deliberately separates instances onto different racks to limit correlated failure, which lengthens the network path between them.

options.text: Launch the 12 instances into a single cluster placement group inside the Availability Zone
options.why: Correct — a cluster placement group packs instances close together on the same high-bisection-bandwidth network segment, giving the lowest latency between tightly coupled nodes.

options.text: Launch the 12 instances into a partition placement group with each partition holding one node
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: partition placement groups isolate racks for distributed data stores, so they trade the very network proximity this simulation depends on.

options.text: Launch four instances in each of three Availability Zones to shorten the paths between them
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: spreading across zones raises availability but sends traffic between separate data centres, adding latency rather than removing it.

questions.stem: A company runs a single AWS account shared by four product teams and cannot tell which team drives which part of the bill. Leadership wants a per-team breakdown of last quarter's spend that they can view and filter, plus an email alert whenever a team's monthly spend crosses an agreed threshold. Which two steps together deliver this? (Select TWO.)
questions.hint: Separate the job of labelling spend by owner from the job of watching that spend against a limit.

options.text: Move each product team into its own VPC inside the shared account.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: a VPC is a network boundary, not a billing dimension, so the invoice looks exactly the same afterwards.

options.text: Apply a team cost allocation tag to resources and activate it in billing.
options.why: Correct — activated cost allocation tags let Cost Explorer group and filter historical spend by the team that owns each resource.

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail data events so every API call made by a team is recorded.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: CloudTrail shows who called which API but carries no pricing data, so it cannot break down a bill.

options.text: Set an IAM permissions boundary that blocks launches above a spend limit.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: permissions boundaries cap which IAM actions are allowed and cannot evaluate accumulated spending.

options.text: Create an AWS Budgets cost budget per team with an email alert threshold.
options.why: Correct — a budget per team compares actual and forecast spend against the agreed threshold and sends the notification when it is crossed.

questions.stem: Administrators need interactive shell access to EC2 instances in private subnets. Security requires that no inbound port is open on the instances, that no SSH key pairs are distributed or rotated, and that every session is attributable to a named identity. Which solution fits best?
questions.hint: Look for the option where the instance starts the connection outbound rather than accepting one.

options.text: Deploy a bastion host in a public subnet and permit SSH from the office CIDR range.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: a bastion is a common pattern, but it still requires an open inbound SSH port and SSH keys that must be distributed and rotated.

options.text: Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with the SSM Agent on the instances.
options.why: Correct — the agent makes an outbound connection to Systems Manager, so no inbound port or key pair is needed, and sessions are authorized by IAM and logged in CloudTrail.

options.text: Give each private instance a public IP and restrict SSH by security group.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: narrowing the source range still leaves an inbound port open and moves the instances out of the private-subnet design.

options.text: Use EC2 user data to install an SSH server listening on port 2222 instead.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: changing the port is obscurity, not security. An inbound listener remains open and key management is unchanged.

questions.stem: A media company distributes static files through an Amazon CloudFront distribution whose origin is an S3 bucket. If that bucket starts returning HTTP 5xx errors, CloudFront must automatically retrieve the same file from a backup bucket in another Region, without any DNS change and without clients using a different domain name. Which configuration meets this requirement?
questions.hint: Think about how one distribution can be given a second origin to try for the same request.

options.text: Create a second distribution for the backup bucket and give its domain name to clients.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: clients would have to switch domain names during an outage, which is exactly the manual step the company ruled out.

options.text: Enable Cross-Region Replication between the two buckets so that both copies always hold the same objects.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: replication keeps the backup bucket current and is a sensible prerequisite, but nothing in it redirects a failed request.

options.text: Create an origin group with both buckets and fail over on 5xx responses from the primary.
options.why: Correct — an origin group lets CloudFront retry the request against the secondary origin when the primary returns one of the configured failure status codes.

options.text: Increase the cache time to live so that cached objects keep serving while the origin is failing.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: a longer TTL only delays revalidation of objects already cached at an edge; a miss still goes to the failing origin and returns the error.

questions.stem: A multiplayer game runs on EC2 behind a Network Load Balancer in us-east-1 and exchanges small TCP messages unique to each player, so nothing can be cached. Players in Europe and Australia report latency that is both high and unpredictable. The fleet must stay in us-east-1. What should the architect deploy?
questions.hint: The traffic is dynamic and per-user, so consider what can shorten and stabilise the network path itself.

options.text: Create a CloudFront distribution that caches the game traffic at edge locations worldwide
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: CloudFront accelerates delivery by caching reusable content, and per-player messages are unique, so no cache hit is ever possible.

options.text: Create Route 53 latency-based records that steer players to the closest endpoint
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: latency-based routing picks among endpoints in several Regions, but only one Region exists here, so every player lands in us-east-1 anyway.

options.text: Create an AWS Global Accelerator and register the Network Load Balancer as its endpoint
options.why: Correct — Global Accelerator gives static anycast addresses that admit players at the nearest edge and carry traffic over the AWS backbone, cutting and steadying long-haul latency.

options.text: Add larger instances and more targets behind the existing Network Load Balancer in the Region
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: extra capacity helps when servers are the bottleneck, yet the delay described comes from the internet path rather than from server load.

questions.topic: Auto Scaling to match a daily demand pattern
questions.stem: A retailer runs its web tier on a fixed fleet of 20 EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. Traffic follows a clear daily pattern, heavy from 09:00 to 18:00 on weekdays and very light overnight and at weekends, with the occasional unplanned surge. The fleet is sized for the busiest hour, so most instances sit idle for two-thirds of every day. Which two changes reduce cost while keeping the site responsive? (Select TWO.)
questions.hint: Consider how capacity can shrink on a pattern you already know and still react to something you did not plan for.

options.text: Buy three-year Reserved Instances covering all 20 fleet instances.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: reserving the full peak discounts capacity that is idle most of the day instead of switching that capacity off.

options.text: Put the web tier in an Auto Scaling group with a target tracking policy on CPU.
options.why: Correct — target tracking adds instances when utilisation rises and removes them when it falls, so unplanned surges are covered without paying for idle hosts.

options.text: Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer to reduce hourly charges.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: the two load balancer types differ in protocol handling, and neither one affects the cost of idle instances.

options.text: Add a scheduled scaling action that lowers the minimum size each evening.
options.why: Correct — the daily pattern is known in advance, so scheduled scaling shrinks the fleet before the quiet period rather than waiting for metrics to react.

options.text: Move the 20 instances to larger types so fewer of them are needed overnight.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: bigger instances cost more per hour, so the same running capacity in fewer, larger hosts does not lower the overnight bill.

questions.stem: An application reads a database password at runtime. Compliance requires the password to be rotated every 30 days by an AWS managed process, with no application code change and no restart. The team wants to avoid writing and operating its own rotation scheduler. Which store should hold the password?
questions.hint: Only one of these services offers built-in scheduled rotation integrated with database credentials.

options.text: An encrypted S3 object that the application reads at start-up each morning.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: an encrypted object can hold the value, but rotation would be custom-built and the read-at-start-up model requires a restart.

options.text: An environment variable on the instance, updated by a monthly manual task.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: environment variables are readable by processes on the host, and a manual monthly step is neither managed nor reliable.

options.text: AWS Secrets Manager, which rotates the secret on a managed schedule for you.
options.why: Correct — Secrets Manager provides built-in rotation using a managed Lambda function for supported databases, and applications retrieve the current value at call time.

options.text: A Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString parameter encrypted by a KMS key.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: SecureString gives encryption and access control, but Parameter Store has no built-in rotation engine for database credentials.

questions.stem: A document-sharing application runs on Linux EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group spread across two Availability Zones behind a load balancer. Uploaded files are written to each instance's own EBS volume, so a file uploaded through one instance is missing when the user is later routed to another instance, and files vanish when the group replaces an instance. Every instance must read and write the same files, and the storage must stay available if one Availability Zone fails. Which storage option meets these requirements?
questions.hint: Consider which AWS storage service many Linux instances in different Availability Zones can mount at the same time.

options.text: Attach one Amazon EBS volume to all of the instances so they share a block device.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: an EBS volume exists in a single Availability Zone and normally attaches to one instance, so it cannot back a fleet spread across two zones.

options.text: Store the files on an Amazon EFS file system that all of the instances mount at boot.
options.why: Correct — EFS is a Regional shared file system that thousands of instances in different Availability Zones can mount concurrently, so all instances see the same files after any replacement.

options.text: Copy new files between the instances with a scheduled job that runs every five minutes.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: files are missing until the next copy runs, and any file written just before an instance is replaced is never copied anywhere.

options.text: Write the files to the instance store volume on each instance for lower latency.
