options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: instance store is ephemeral local disk that is discarded when the instance stops and is never readable by other instances.

questions.stem: A ticketing service stores orders in DynamoDB. Traffic is near zero for days, then jumps to many thousands of writes per second within seconds of a sale opening, and requests are currently rejected with throttling errors during those spikes. Which two approaches let the table absorb the bursts? (Select TWO.)
questions.hint: Focus on the mechanisms that change how much write capacity the table itself can supply.

options.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode so it serves the traffic that arrives
options.why: Correct — on-demand mode requires no capacity planning and scales the table up to sustain sudden bursts, charging per request rather than per provisioned unit.

options.text: Keep provisioned mode and attach auto scaling policies to the table write capacity
options.why: Correct — application auto scaling raises provisioned write units as consumption climbs and lowers them when the sale ends, so the table follows demand instead of a fixed ceiling.

options.text: Create a DynamoDB Accelerator cluster in front of the table to take the spikes
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: DAX caches read results and writes still pass through to the table, so it does nothing for a burst made up of order writes.

options.text: Add a global secondary index so that write requests are shared across two separate indexes
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: a GSI consumes its own write capacity for every item written, so adding one increases the write cost of the spike rather than relieving it.

options.text: Enable point-in-time recovery on the table so throttled writes are replayed automatically
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: point-in-time recovery protects against data loss by keeping backups, and it neither adds capacity nor retries requests that were rejected.

questions.topic: Serverless as a cost model for idle workloads
questions.stem: A small team runs two always-on t3.medium EC2 instances. One hosts a REST API that handles about 20,000 requests a day in short unpredictable bursts; the other runs a single nightly batch job that completes in six minutes. Both instances are billed for all 24 hours even though they do useful work for a small fraction of the day, and the team wants to stop paying for idle time without managing servers. Which two changes achieve that? (Select TWO.)
questions.hint: Look for services billed per invocation and per millisecond of execution rather than per running hour.

options.text: Move the REST API to AWS Lambda functions behind Amazon API Gateway.
options.why: Correct — Lambda bills only for invocations and execution time, so bursty traffic costs nothing between requests and needs no servers to manage.

options.text: Buy one-year Reserved Instances covering both t3.medium instances.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: a reservation lowers the hourly rate but the team is still billed around the clock for capacity that is mostly idle.

options.text: Run the nightly job as a Lambda function triggered by an EventBridge rule.
options.why: Correct — a six-minute job fits well inside the Lambda timeout, and a scheduled rule invokes it so nothing is billed for the other 23 hours.

options.text: Resize both instances to t3.small and keep them running all the time.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: a smaller instance simply charges a lower hourly rate, so the team keeps paying for every idle hour.

options.text: Place both instances in an Auto Scaling group with a minimum size of two hosts.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: a minimum of two pins the same pair of instances in place, so the group never removes the idle capacity.

questions.stem: A public website served by an Application Load Balancer must be reachable over HTTPS using a certificate trusted by browsers. The certificate must renew automatically at no additional charge, and the team wants no manual certificate installation on servers. What should the architect do?
questions.hint: Consider where the certificate has to live for a managed service to renew it for you.

options.text: Request a public ACM certificate and attach it to an HTTPS listener on the ALB.
options.why: Correct — public certificates issued by ACM are free, deploy directly to integrated services such as ALB, and are renewed automatically while validation remains in place.

options.text: Purchase a certificate from a third-party CA and install it on every EC2 instance.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: this does produce a trusted certificate, but renewal and installation stay manual and must be repeated on every instance.

options.text: Import a self-signed certificate into ACM and attach it to the load balancer.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: browsers do not trust self-signed certificates, and ACM never renews imported certificates automatically.

options.text: Enable server-side encryption on the target group so traffic is encrypted.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: server-side encryption protects data at rest in storage services; target groups have no such setting and it would not secure traffic in transit.

questions.stem: Customers of a shopping site are signed out at random times and lose the contents of their carts. The site runs on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and each instance holds session data in its own memory, so sessions disappear whenever the group scales in or replaces an instance. Sessions must survive the loss of any single instance without changing how customers reach the site. What should a solutions architect recommend?
questions.hint: Think about where session data must live for any instance in the fleet to be able to read it.

options.text: Turn on sticky sessions so the load balancer returns each customer to one instance.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: stickiness keeps a customer on the instance that holds the session, but the session is still destroyed when that instance goes away.

options.text: Lengthen the Auto Scaling cooldown period so instances are removed less frequently.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: scaling in less often reduces how frequently sessions are lost, yet a crash or a health check failure still wipes them out.

options.text: Keep session data in an Amazon ElastiCache cluster shared by all the instances.
options.why: Correct — moving session state to an external in-memory store makes the instances stateless, so any instance can serve any customer and no session is tied to a server's lifetime.

options.text: Write session data to a separate Amazon EBS volume attached to each instance.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: EBS is block storage bound to one instance, so a session written by one server cannot be read by the others in the group.

questions.stem: An order site calls an image-rendering service synchronously on every checkout. During flash sales the renderers cannot keep up, requests time out, and orders are lost, even though rendering may finish minutes later. Which two changes let the site accept every order during a burst? (Select TWO.)
questions.hint: Think about what a buffer between the two tiers gives you, and what the workers should then scale on.

options.text: Have the web tier write each render job to an SQS queue and return to the shopper
options.why: Correct — the queue accepts every job at burst speed and holds it durably, so the web tier stops waiting on renderers and no order is dropped when they fall behind.

options.text: Run the renderers in an Auto Scaling group scaled on the number of messages in the queue
options.why: Correct — queue depth is the direct signal of backlog, so scaling renderer instances on it adds workers while the burst is draining and removes them afterwards.

options.text: Raise the connection timeout on the web tier so each checkout waits for its render to finish
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: longer timeouts only make shoppers wait, and holding thousands of open connections exhausts web tier resources instead of adding rendering capacity.

options.text: Add an Application Load Balancer in front of the renderer fleet to spread load
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: even spreading is good practice, but a fixed renderer fleet still receives more work than it can process during the sale.

options.text: Store each rendered image in S3 so finished output is durable and cheap to serve later
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: S3 is the right home for finished images, yet it changes nothing about how the burst of render requests is accepted or absorbed.

questions.stem: A company runs 30 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations. Employees should sign in once with their existing corporate directory credentials and then receive role-based access to only the accounts they need, without an IAM user being created in each account. Which approach should the architect choose?
questions.hint: Think about which service assigns reusable role definitions across many accounts from one place.

options.text: Amazon Cognito user pools, to give employees console sign-in.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: Cognito is built for customer-facing application sign-in, not for workforce access to the AWS Management Console across accounts.

options.text: An IAM user in each account for every employee, with a shared password policy.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: this grants access but multiplies identities across 30 accounts and duplicates joiner and leaver work in each one.

options.text: AWS IAM Identity Center, with permission sets mapped to directory groups.
options.why: Correct — Identity Center federates the corporate directory once, then provisions roles from permission sets into member accounts based on group assignment.

options.text: A service control policy in each account that grants employees console access.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: SCPs only limit the maximum permissions in an account. They never grant access and they do not authenticate anyone.

questions.stem: A company keeps application data on Amazon EBS volumes attached to EC2 instances in eu-west-1. The business now requires that this data can be rebuilt in a second AWS Region if eu-west-1 becomes unavailable, and it accepts losing up to 24 hours of the most recent data. The team wants to rely on native Amazon EBS capabilities rather than third-party replication software. Which TWO actions together meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
questions.hint: Remember which Region an EBS snapshot is stored in, and what has to happen before it can be used elsewhere.

options.text: Create a snapshot of every volume once a day on an automated schedule.
options.why: Correct — a daily snapshot captures a consistent point-in-time copy of the volume, which keeps the worst-case data loss inside the accepted 24-hour window.

options.text: Copy each new snapshot to the second Region so volumes can be created there.
options.why: Correct — snapshots are stored in the Region where they were taken, so copying them to the second Region is what makes the data restorable after eu-west-1 is lost.

options.text: Enable EBS Multi-Attach so the volume is reachable from the second Region.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: Multi-Attach lets several instances in one Availability Zone use the same volume and moves no data between Regions.

options.text: Take a snapshot of each volume only before every application release.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: releases can be weeks apart, so the gap between recovery points would be far longer than the 24 hours the business accepts.

options.text: Change the volumes to the gp3 volume type so that their stored data becomes more durable.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: volume type sets performance and price characteristics; it does not create recovery points or place a copy of the data anywhere else.

questions.stem: A clickstream pipeline sends events to a Kinesis data stream with four shards. Producers now generate far more than 4 MB per second, write calls are throttled, and metrics show one shard receiving most records because the partition key is the country code. Which two changes raise ingest throughput? (Select TWO.)
questions.hint: Stream capacity is per shard, so consider both how many shards exist and how evenly records land on them.

options.text: Increase the shard count on the stream so total write capacity grows with it
options.why: Correct — each shard accepts 1 MB or 1,000 records per second, so adding shards raises the stream's aggregate write ceiling in proportion.

options.text: Use a high-cardinality partition key such as the session identifier for each record
options.why: Correct — a key with many distinct values distributes records evenly across shards, removing the hot shard that throttles writes while other shards sit idle.

options.text: Extend the stream data retention period from 24 hours to seven days
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: longer retention gives consumers more time to re-read records, but it leaves the per-shard write limit exactly where it was.

options.text: Replace the stream with an SQS FIFO queue so that events are processed in strict order
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: SQS FIFO guarantees ordering and exactly-once handling, not high-volume parallel ingest with multiple independent stream readers.

options.text: Register an enhanced fan-out consumer so each consumer gets its own read throughput
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: enhanced fan-out enlarges the read side per consumer, and the throttling described is on producer writes into the shards.

questions.stem: A company new to AWS runs its workloads on Amazon EC2 and wants to know exactly which recurring security task remains its own job rather than AWS's, under the AWS shared responsibility model. Which task is the customer's responsibility?
questions.hint: Draw the line at the boundary between the virtualization layer and what the customer launches on top of it.

options.text: Replacing failed disks in the AWS data centre storage racks.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: hardware maintenance is part of security of the cloud and is performed by AWS; the customer never touches physical media.

options.text: Installing operating system security patches on their EC2 instances.
options.why: Correct — with EC2 the guest operating system, its patches, and everything installed above it are security in the cloud, which is the customer's responsibility.

options.text: Patching the hypervisor software that runs underneath EC2 instances.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: the virtualization layer is managed by AWS and is not reachable or patchable by customers.

options.text: Controlling physical access to AWS Regions, data centres and their hardware.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: physical security is a genuine and audited control, but AWS owns it entirely, so it is never a customer task.

questions.stem: An order service currently posts each new order over HTTP to one processing fleet. Three independent downstream systems for billing, shipping, and analytics now each need their own copy of every order event. Each system is taken offline for maintenance from time to time and must still process the orders raised while it was down, and the order service must send each order only once. Which TWO actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)
questions.hint: Separate the job of delivering one event to many subscribers from the job of holding events for a consumer that is absent.

options.text: Publish each order once to an Amazon SNS topic instead of to the three systems.
options.why: Correct — a topic delivers one published message to every subscriber, so the order service writes the event a single time and the three systems each receive a copy.

options.text: Have the order service post every order to each system's endpoint in turn.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: the sender repeats the work three times and an order aimed at a system that is offline is simply lost.

options.text: Subscribe one Amazon SQS queue for each of the downstream systems to the topic.
options.why: Correct — each queue stores its copy of the message until that system polls and deletes it, so orders raised during a maintenance window are processed afterwards.

options.text: Subscribe the three HTTP endpoints to an Amazon SNS topic and rely on its delivery retries.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: retries cover brief network glitches, but nothing holds the events for a system that stays offline through a maintenance window.

options.text: Send every order to a single Amazon SQS queue that all three systems poll.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: one consumer receives and deletes a given message, so the three systems would share the orders instead of each getting a copy.

questions.stem: A mobile application must let users register and sign in with an email address and password, and must also allow existing users to sign in with their Google accounts. After sign-in, the application must call Amazon DynamoDB directly with signed requests using short-lived AWS credentials scoped by an IAM role. Which two Amazon Cognito components address these needs? (Select TWO.)
questions.hint: Separate the job of authenticating a user from the job of handing out AWS credentials.

options.text: A Cognito user pool that handles sign-up, sign-in and Google federation.
options.why: Correct — a user pool is the user directory: it stores registered users, runs the sign-in flow, supports social identity providers such as Google, and returns JWT tokens.

options.text: A Cognito identity pool that exchanges tokens for temporary AWS credentials.
options.why: Correct — an identity pool takes the token from the user pool and calls STS, returning temporary credentials tied to an IAM role so the app can sign AWS API calls.

options.text: An AWS Directory Service directory joined by each device.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: Directory Service provides Microsoft Active Directory for enterprise workloads and domain-joined servers, not consumer mobile sign-in.

options.text: An IAM user created per application user, with keys embedded in the app.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: IAM is not designed for large consumer user bases, and shipping access keys inside a mobile app exposes them to anyone who inspects it.

options.text: An IAM Identity Center permission set assigned to every mobile application user.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: permission sets serve workforce access to AWS accounts and consoles, not end users of a public consumer application.

questions.topic: Auto Scaling capacity for AZ loss
questions.stem: A web tier runs on four EC2 instances in one Availability Zone in an Auto Scaling group whose minimum, desired, and maximum capacity are all set to four, and all four instances are needed to carry peak traffic. The Application Load Balancer in front of the fleet already has subnets enabled in two Availability Zones. The business now requires the site to keep serving peak traffic even while one Availability Zone is unavailable. Which TWO changes should a solutions architect make? (Select TWO.)
questions.hint: Consider both where the instances are launched and how much capacity is still running once one zone disappears.

options.text: Replace the four instances with two instances of twice the size in the same zone.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: the fleet keeps the same total capacity but all of it still sits in the one zone whose loss the business is worried about.

options.text: Extend the Auto Scaling group to use subnets in both of the Availability Zones.
options.why: Correct — a group with subnets in two zones balances its instances across them, so losing one zone removes only part of the fleet instead of all of it.

options.text: Launch the instances into a cluster placement group for higher network throughput.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: a cluster placement group packs instances into a single Availability Zone, which works against surviving the loss of that zone.

options.text: Raise the minimum and desired capacity of the group to eight running instances.
options.why: Correct — with eight instances split evenly across two zones, the four that remain in the surviving zone are still enough to carry the full peak load.

options.text: Enable termination protection on the instances so they cannot be shut down.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: termination protection only rejects the terminate API call and offers nothing when the Availability Zone itself becomes unavailable.

questions.stem: An external auditing firm, which has its own AWS account, needs read-only access to resources in your account for a two-week engagement. Your policy forbids creating IAM users for third parties and forbids sharing any access keys outside the company. Which two actions together provide this access? (Select TWO.)
questions.hint: Think about which document names who may assume an identity and which API hands back short-lived keys.

options.text: Create an IAM role with a read-only policy and a trust policy for their account.
options.why: Correct — the permissions policy defines what the auditors can do, and the trust policy names the external account as the principal allowed to assume the role.

options.text: Add the auditors' account to a resource-based policy on every EC2 instance.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: EC2 instances do not support resource-based policies, so there is nothing to attach a cross-account grant to.

options.text: Have the auditors assume that role with STS to obtain temporary credentials.
options.why: Correct — AssumeRole returns short-lived credentials that expire on their own, so no long-lived key leaves the account and access lapses when the engagement ends.

options.text: Create an IAM user for each auditor and mail the generated access keys to them.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: this is the pattern the requirement explicitly forbids, and emailed long-lived keys are hard to revoke and easy to leak.

options.text: Enable AWS Organizations and invite the auditing firm's account into the organization.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: joining an organization is for accounts you own and govern; it grants no read access by itself and is far too broad for a two-week audit.

questions.stem: A security team has two goals. First, it must find out whether any Amazon S3 bucket in the account holds customer credit card numbers. Second, it wants an alert when an EC2 instance begins communicating with a known command-and-control domain. Both must come from managed services that need no agent installation. Which two services meet these goals? (Select TWO.)
questions.hint: One goal is about what the stored data contains; the other is about how a resource is behaving on the network.

options.text: AWS WAF, to filter web requests by rules before they reach an application.
options.why: Wrong — right-service-wrong-feature: WAF inspects inbound HTTP requests at CloudFront or a load balancer; it neither scans stored data nor watches outbound instance traffic.

options.text: Amazon Macie, to discover and classify sensitive data held in S3 buckets.
options.why: Correct — Macie uses managed data identifiers to find sensitive values such as payment card numbers in S3 objects and reports which buckets contain them.

options.text: Amazon Inspector, to scan instances for known software vulnerabilities.
options.why: Wrong — valid-but-inferior-here: Inspector is a useful continuous scanner, but it reports CVEs and unintended network reachability, not live malicious communication.

options.text: Amazon GuardDuty, to flag suspicious network and API activity in the account.
options.why: Correct — GuardDuty analyses VPC flow logs, DNS logs and CloudTrail events, raising findings such as an instance contacting a known command-and-control endpoint.

options.text: AWS Shield Standard, to absorb network layer distributed denial of service floods.
options.why: Wrong — common-misconception: Shield Standard mitigates inbound volumetric attacks automatically; it performs no data classification and no behavioural detection.

questions.stem: An auditor asks for two separate things about security groups in an AWS account over the past year: a timeline showing how each security group's rules changed over time, and evidence of which principal made each change and from which source IP address. Which two services should the team rely on? (Select TWO.)
questions.hint: One service answers what the resource looked like; the other answers who called the API.

options.text: VPC Flow Logs, to capture accepted and rejected subnet traffic.
options.why: Wrong — true-but-doesn't-answer-it: flow logs show the traffic a security group allowed or dropped, but they record no configuration changes and no API callers.

options.text: AWS Config, to record the configuration history of the security groups.
options.why: Correct — Config records a timestamped configuration item each time a recorded resource changes, giving the required timeline and point-in-time views.

options.text: AWS CloudTrail, to log the API calls and the identity that made them.
options.why: Correct — CloudTrail events include the principal, the source IP address, the time and the parameters of each management API call such as AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress.

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch alarms, to notify the team when a metric crosses a limit.
